clue.text: Fools follow PM on air, making case for growth?

indicators.note: something said on air is broadcast and heard, so these words are to be pronounced rather than written

parts.note: PM is Prime Minister Theresa May (in office when this was set), and fools, as a verb, means plays tricks: so TRICKS after MAY

explanation.surface: Jokers trail a Prime Minister during a broadcast, which becomes a cultivating medium for something growing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making' is a link word. A matrix is a mould or womb in which something develops, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A matrix is the surrounding medium or mould in which something forms and develops, like a womb.

clue.text: Old soldiers have to track round half of Kent

indicators.note: the word for must goes round the piece of Kent

parts.note: must means have to

indicators.note: the first half of the word Kent, its opening two letters

parts.note: RY abbreviates railway, a track

explanation.surface: Veteran troops must follow a track around part of the English county of Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Musketry is musket fire, and collectively the musketeers or old infantrymen who used it.

clue.text: Definitely don't shuffle or hit ball

parts.note: to tap is to hit lightly
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Firm advice not to mix the cards, or to strike a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' is a link word. 'Shuffle' suggests cards, but it is a dance step; a tap dance is lively, the opposite of a shuffling walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhythmic routine of loud foot clicks is the very opposite of a quiet, lazy shuffling gait.

clue.text: Paid less essentially?

indicators.note: the essence is the core, so the central letters of these words

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone is underpaid, essentially.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also hints at the sense: someone not working earns less.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of work, not employed, would leave someone with lower pay.

clue.text: Verse, one of five impressing a West End academician

indicators.note: to impress is to press something into, so the quintuplet holds the next pieces within

parts.note: a quin is a quintuplet, one of five babies born together

indicators.note: the end of the word West, its closing letter

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: Poetry about a quintuplet making an impression on a theatre-district artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district but gives only the last letter of West.
explanation.definitionFit: A quatrain is a stanza of four lines, so a kind of verse.

clue.text: Indifferent coach enters boring team

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the rearranged letters go inside the team

parts.note: United is a common football team name, such as Manchester United

indicators.note: to coach is to train or reshape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A manager who doesn't care joins a dull football team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like a synonym for dull, but here it means drilling into; 'coach' signals the rearrangement of 'enters'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uninterested has no curiosity or concern, so is indifferent.

clue.text: Deal with college running labour group

parts.note: to trade is to deal
uni is short for university, a college
on means running, operating

explanation.surface: A business deal with a college that runs a workers' association.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade union is an organised association of workers.

clue.text: Writer's obsessed cradling pig

indicators.note: to cradle is to hold within the arms, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: anal means obsessively fussy
the writer, the setter, says I'M for I am

explanation.surface: A writer is obsessed with holding a pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Mainly unwarranted hype

indicators.note: the main part of the word, so its tail is trimmed

parts.note: needless means unwarranted, unnecessary

explanation.surface: Largely unjustified publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hype' is short for hypodermic, not publicity.
explanation.definitionFit: A hype is a slang shortening of hypodermic, the sharp hollow spike of a syringe.

clue.text: Drink and work flexibly

parts.note: to sup is to drink
to ply a trade is to work at it

explanation.surface: Someone has a drink and keeps flexible working hours.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer here is the adverb from supple, not the noun meaning provision.
explanation.definitionFit: Supply is the adverb of supple, meaning in a pliant, bendy manner.

clue.text: Boxer's breaking superb clinch

indicators.note: breaking into a word means getting inside it, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: fine means excellent, superb
Ali is the boxer Muhammad Ali, with the possessive S

explanation.surface: A boxer's superb clinch in the ring is broken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clinch' suggests a boxing hold, but here it is the verb meaning settle a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: To clinch a deal is to settle or complete it conclusively.

clue.text: Person supervising ring binder about chief suspect

parts.note: O is ring-shaped

indicators.note: the binder goes about, around, the rearranged letters

parts.note: a folder is a binder for papers

indicators.note: suspect means doubtful, not right, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Someone in charge rings a binder about the main suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chief suspect' reads like a police phrase, but 'suspect' is the signal to rearrange 'chief'; 'about' means the binder wraps around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who holds an office occupies a position of authority, overseeing others.

clue.text: Line in each number shows flair

indicators.note: the line is placed in the middle of the abbreviation for each

parts.note: N is the mathematical symbol for a number

explanation.surface: A line within each number displays artistic panache.
explanation.definitionFit: Elan is vigorous style and dash, a synonym of flair.

clue.text: Wacky way to play squash?

definitions.meaning: squash shots are struck so that the ball rebounds from the court's front surface

explanation.surface: An eccentric method of playing the racket sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means crazy or unconventional, and literally describes balls bouncing back in squash.

clue.text: What keeper wants that depresses author?

definitions.text: What keeper wants that depresses author?

parts.words: What keeper wants that depresses author?
parts.note: a goalkeeper hopes to concede no goals, while a writer facing blank, unmarked paper feels writer's block

explanation.surface: Something a goalkeeper desires but that gets a writer down.
explanation.walkthrough: In football a game with no goals conceded is credited to the keeper; the same phrase is a blank page.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both a match without conceding and an unwritten page.

clue.text: Mostly remember tirade about citation that's perverse

indicators.note: most of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: to recall is to remember
cit. is an abbreviation for citation
a rant is a tirade

explanation.surface: Someone half-recalls a harangue over a quotation, and finds it contrary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is a link word here: the rant concerns the citation. 'That's' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Recalcitrant means stubbornly uncooperative, which is what perverse describes.

clue.text: Software runs cricket ground OK

parts.note: an app is a piece of software
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
the Oval is a London cricket ground

explanation.surface: A program tallies runs, and the cricket ground is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a Test cricket ground in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving the OK means giving consent, sanction.

clue.text: Hard to grasp drunk in east Morecambe

indicators.note: the drunkard goes in between the two other pieces

parts.note: Eric Morecambe was a much-loved British comedian, half of Morecambe and Wise
a sot is a drunk

explanation.surface: Something obscure happening with a drunk in the east of Morecambe, a Lancashire seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe looks like the town, but it is the comedian Eric Morecambe.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric means understood only by a select few, so obscure.

clue.text: Rebus has a cop trained in order to appear in court

indicators.note: trained means shaped or drilled into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Inspector Rebus, Ian Rankin's Edinburgh detective, has a police officer trained up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link word. Rebus is a fictional Scottish police inspector, which makes the legal theme seem natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Habeas corpus is a writ requiring a detained person to be brought before a judge.

clue.text: MacKenzie's poorly, shedding skin, due to this?

definitions.text: MacKenzie's poorly, shedding skin, due to this?

indicators.note: poorly means unwell, out of sorts, so the letters are disordered
shedding means casting off, so the letters of the second word are taken away from the first

explanation.surface: Someone named MacKenzie is unwell and losing skin, perhaps because of this.
explanation.walkthrough: Take S, K, I, N from MACKENZIES and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Eczema is a skin condition causing inflamed, flaking, itchy patches.

clue.text: Where to find stiff chap briefly stopping extra

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so one piece is placed in the other

parts.note: more means extra

indicators.note: briefly means shortened, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a guy is a chap

explanation.surface: Where you'd find a rigid fellow, cut short while halting an extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' is slang for a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A morgue is a mortuary, where dead bodies are kept.

clue.text: Angry doctor often portrayed with skull

parts.note: cross means annoyed, angry
Bones is the nickname of Dr McCoy in Star Trek, a stock crossword doctor

explanation.surface: An irate doctor frequently depicted beside a skull, like a medical portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossed bones appear with a skull on the pirate flag and warning signs.

clue.text: Worry about filling this paper

indicators.note: one piece fills the other, sitting inside it

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, the paper the puzzle appears in
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Anxiety over what fills this newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret is to be anxious, to worry.

clue.text: Maybe author pens The Dandy

indicators.note: pens means encloses, so the answer is held within these words

explanation.surface: Perhaps a writer contributes to The Dandy, a long-running British children's comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' is a link word. The Dandy was a British comic.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is a fashionable man who is particular about dress, a dandy.

clue.text: Quiz experts beaten at breakfast?

explanation.surface: Clever quiz champions defeated over the breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: Eggheads is a British TV quiz in which challengers try to beat a panel of experts; 'beaten' also suggests eggs being bashed or whisked at breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Intellectuals are nicknamed for bald domed foreheads, and the BBC quiz show uses this name for its expert panel.

clue.text: He tends to loom and dither over everything at first

indicators.note: the dithering word goes over, covering, the single letter, so it sits within

parts.note: to waver is to dither, hesitate

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word everything

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loom' looks like a verb meaning tower; it is the noun, a weaving frame that the answer tends.
explanation.definitionFit: A weaver works at a loom, tending the machine that makes cloth.

clue.text: Opening a smart university about to close

indicators.note: to close means at the close, the end, of the answer

parts.note: pert means smart, jaunty
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A smart university is opening, but about to close.

clue.text: Prominent suburbs of Dublin missing in postcard

indicators.note: the inner letters go in the abbreviation for postcard

parts.note: PC abbreviates postcard

indicators.note: suburbs lie on a city's outskirts, here the outer letters of the word Dublin
those outer letters are left out, leaving its interior
